item.text:
**Audit Result**
The defensible final accepted set is **20 sources**. That meets the target without counting context-only items, and it removes every mirror/reprint and duplicate-family record from the provisional 31 opened-and-accepted set.

**Accepted Ledger**
- `S001` [Report on Violations and Abuses of International Humanitarian and Human Rights Law, War Crimes and Crimes Against Humanity related to the Forcible Transfer and/or Deportation of Ukrainian Children to the Russian Federation](https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/542751) | OSCE ODIHR | 2023-05-04 | source type: OSCE expert mission report page | confidence: high, because it is an official OSCE mission/report page on a specific 2023 fact pattern | final evidence use: child deportation, occupation coercion, IHL, accountability | language: English | locator: `turn16view1` L61-L69 | supported claims: OSCE expert mission report addresses forcible transfer/deportation of Ukrainian children to the Russian Federation | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect via Russian state/occupation policy | limitations: landing-page summary, not a court judgment | contrary considerations: allegation framing, not conviction | lenses: L2, L4, L5, L9, L10
- `S002` [OSCE human rights office monitoring finds evidence of torture and sexual violence in Ukraine as violations continue](https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/548662) | OSCE ODIHR | 2023-07-17 | source type: OSCE monitoring summary | confidence: high | final evidence use: civilian abuse, detention abuse, accountability | language: English | locator: `turn16view2` L75-L84 | supported claims: arbitrary imprisonment, enforced disappearances, torture, sexual violence, summary executions, forcible displacement, and attacks on civilians/civilian objects | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect via Russian armed forces and occupation structures | limitations: monitoring summary, not a criminal finding | contrary considerations: also notes abuse allegations involving Russian POWs | lenses: L2, L4, L5, L9, L10
- `S003` [Report on Violations and Abuses of International Humanitarian and Human Rights Law, War Crimes and Crimes Against Humanity related to the Treatment of Ukrainian Children](https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/541829) | OSCE ODIHR | 2023-05-30 | source type: OSCE interim report | confidence: high | final evidence use: child-transfer pattern, occupation coercion, accountability | language: English | locator: `turn22view5` L62-L84 | supported claims: ongoing OSCE fact-finding on the treatment of Ukrainian children documents coercive Russian practices and legal concerns | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect via Russian state/occupation policy | limitations: expert fact-finding, not adjudication | contrary considerations: report language is evidentiary, not judicial | lenses: L2, L4, L5, L9, L10
- `S004` [Update on the human rights situation in Ukraine, 1 February 2023 - 30 April 2023](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/update-human-rights-situation-ukraine-1-february-2023-30-april-2023-EN) | OHCHR / HRMMU | 2023-06-13 | source type: UN human rights report | confidence: high | final evidence use: passportization, occupation coercion, religious repression | language: English | locator: `turn22view2` L81-L84 | supported claims: a Putin decree pressured occupied residents toward Russian passports and exposed some to deportation/forcible transfer risk; violence against UOC members/supporters increased | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: direct to the President’s decree and occupation framework | limitations: mid-2023 reporting window | contrary considerations: decree does not itself impose citizenship | lenses: L2, L4, L5, L6, L7, L9, L10
- `S005` [Protection of Civilians in Armed Conflict - December 2023](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/protection-civilians-armed-conflict-december-2023-EN) | OHCHR / HRMMU | 2024-01-15 | source type: UN human rights report | confidence: high | final evidence use: year-end civilian casualty trend, strike pattern | language: English | locator: `turn22view1` L82-L85 | supported claims: at least 592 civilians were killed or injured in December 2023; the increase was driven mainly by intensified Russian missile and loitering-munition attacks on 29 and 30 December | temporal fit: reports December 2023 facts | Putin attribution: indirect via Russian armed forces | limitations: published in January 2024, but factual window is December 2023 | contrary considerations: casualties occurred in government-controlled territory too | lenses: L2, L4, L5, L9, L10
- `S006` [Russia - Ukraine international armed conflict: ICRC continues to help people in need](https://www.icrc.org/en/document/russia-ukraine-international-armed-conflict-icrc-continues-help-people-need) | ICRC | 2023-06-14 | source type: humanitarian operational report | confidence: high | final evidence use: civilian protection, humanitarian access, POWs, water, mine risk | language: English | locator: `turn18view5` L218-L236 and `turn18view7` L188-L193 | supported claims: ICRC visited over 1,500 POWs, helped 5,500 families, brought safe drinking water to over 1.9 million people since the start of 2023, and delivered cash aid, food, and hygiene support | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect, as a consequence of the war and occupation conditions | limitations: humanitarian actor, not an attribution body | contrary considerations: emphasizes aid and contact across frontlines rather than blame | lenses: L4, L5, L7, L9, L10
- `S026` [Putin visits Mariupol as part of surprise tour of occupied Ukraine](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/putin-visits-mariupol-as-part-of-surprise-tour-of-occupied-ukraine/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjM6bmV3c21sX1ZBODQ4MTE5MDMyMDIzUlAx) | Reuters Connect | 2023-03-19 | source type: licensable video | confidence: high | final evidence use: occupied-territory control, public justification, coercive consolidation | language: English | locator: Reuters Connect item description and released footage | supported claims: Putin personally visited occupied Mariupol and inspected reconstruction messaging in Russian-controlled territory | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: direct | limitations: video record rather than a narrative transcript | contrary considerations: staged public-relations content, not an independent field report | lenses: L2, L3, L5, L6, L10
- `S027` [Russian Federation: New Law Introduces Electronic Summons for Conscripts](https://www.loc.gov/item/global-legal-monitor/2023-07-10/russian-federation-new-law-introduces-electronic-summons-for-conscripts/) | Library of Congress | 2023-07-11 | source type: legal-monitor summary | confidence: medium-high, because it is a high-authority legal summary of a Putin-signed law rather than the statute text itself | final evidence use: mobilization, draft enforcement, administrative coercion | language: English | locator: `turn24view3` L39-L41 and L52-L57; `turn24view4` L39-L41 | supported claims: Putin signed Federal Law No. 127-FZ on 14 April 2023; it created electronic summons, a unified registry, and penalties/constraints for evaders | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: direct signature | limitations: not the statute text itself | contrary considerations: framed as administrative modernization | lenses: L2, L3, L5, L8, L10
- `S028` [The Secretary-General -- Remarks to the Press](https://ukraine.un.org/en/222286-secretary-general-remarks-press) | United Nations in Ukraine | 2023-03-08 | source type: UN press remarks | confidence: high | final evidence use: diplomacy, ceasefire framing, accountability, humanitarian corridors, POW exchanges, grain corridor | language: English | locator: `turn28view0` L69-L115 | supported claims: a just peace must be based on the UN Charter and international law; UN work included humanitarian aid, Azovstal evacuations, Black Sea grain exports, ZNPP demilitarization, POW exchanges, and accountability | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect through Russia state action | limitations: UN institutional perspective | contrary considerations: acknowledges humanitarian relief and negotiation channels | lenses: L1, L4, L5, L6, L7, L9, L10
- `S034` [Human rights situation during the Russian occupation of territory of Ukraine and its aftermath, 24 February 2022 to 31 December 2023](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/human-rights-situation-during-russian-occupation-territory-ukraine-and-its-aftermath-EN) | OHCHR / HRMMU | 2024-03-20 | source type: thematic UN human rights report | confidence: high | final evidence use: occupation administration, coercion, Russification, accountability | language: English | locator: `turn27view0` L83-L102 | supported claims: systematic dismantling of rights in occupied territory, coercive governance changes, Russian legal framework imposition, passport-based discrimination, forced Russian curriculum, child enlistment, and the need for withdrawal and accountability | temporal fit: covers through 31 Dec 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect but strongly state-policy linked | limitations: retrospective 2024 publication; Russia lacked access to occupied areas | contrary considerations: notes possible overbreadth in some collaboration prosecutions | lenses: L2, L4, L5, L9, L10
- `S036` [Executive Order approving Russia’s Foreign Policy Concept](https://en.special.kremlin.ru/events/president/news/70811) | President of Russia | 2023-31-03 | source type: official presidential decree | confidence: high | final evidence use: Russian self-justification, foreign-policy doctrine, anti-West framing, diplomatic baseline | language: English | locator: decree text and concept text (`turn0search4` / `turn6view0` L96-L116) | supported claims: Putin approved a foreign policy concept describing Russia as миролюбивый/peaceful and opposing Western hegemony, while reserving the right to defend national interests | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: direct signature | limitations: official doctrine, inherently self-serving | contrary considerations: same text also stresses resistance to Western aggression and “all available means” | lenses: L1, L2, L3, L5, L6, L10
- `S037` [NOTE TO CORRESPONDENTS: UN Secretary-General visits Ukraine](https://ukraine.un.org/en/222054-note-correspondents-un-secretary-general-visits-ukraine) | United Nations in Ukraine | 2023-03-07 | source type: UN press note | confidence: high | final evidence use: diplomacy/access, mediation context | language: English | locator: page heading and date | supported claims: Guterres was traveling to Kyiv to discuss continuation of the Black Sea Grain Initiative and related issues | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect through the Russia-Ukraine negotiation context | limitations: procedural note, not a negotiated text | contrary considerations: active UN mediation rather than unilateral escalation | lenses: L1, L7, L10
- `S038` [Note to Correspondents: Update on the Black Sea Grain Initiative](https://ukraine.un.org/en/215728-note-correspondents-update-black-sea-grain-initiative) | United Nations in Ukraine | 2023-01-19 | source type: UN press note | confidence: high | final evidence use: diplomacy, food-security mitigation, humanitarian relief | language: English | locator: page heading and date | supported claims: 17.8 million tonnes exported by 19 Jan 2023; China was the primary recipient; UN urged parties to remove obstacles and expand ammonia/fertilizer facilitation | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect via Russia’s role in the Black Sea framework | limitations: operational note, not a legal finding | contrary considerations: emphasizes continued multilateral cooperation and benefits | lenses: L1, L4, L7, L10
- `S039` [Note to Correspondents: extension of the Black Sea Grain Initiative](https://ukraine.un.org/en/223807-note-correspondents-extension-black-sea-grain-initiative) | United Nations in Ukraine | 2023-03-18 | source type: UN press note | confidence: high | final evidence use: diplomacy and mitigation | language: English | locator: page heading and date | supported claims: the initiative was extended; 25 million metric tonnes had moved to 45 countries; Türkiye provided diplomatic and operational support; the UN urged full implementation | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect via Russia’s participation in the framework | limitations: institutional diplomacy note | contrary considerations: directly credits multilateral continuation rather than rupture | lenses: L1, L4, L7, L10
- `S040` [Note to Correspondents on the Black Sea Grain Initiative](https://ukraine.un.org/en/227225-note-correspondents-black-sea-grain-initiative) | United Nations in Ukraine | 2023-04-11 | source type: UN press note | confidence: high | final evidence use: diplomacy, humanitarian mitigation, operational restraint | language: English | locator: page heading and date | supported claims: inspections paused and resumed after JCC talks; UN and Türkiye were involved; 27.5 million metric tonnes had moved; global food-price relief and humanitarian supply were being sustained | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect via Russian participation in the JCC system | limitations: operational update, not a negotiation transcript | contrary considerations: stresses shared responsibilities and continued coordination | lenses: L1, L4, L7, L10
- `S041` [UN Secretary-General's remarks at press encounter on the Black Sea Initiative](https://ukraine.un.org/en/232006-un-secretary-generals-remarks-press-encounter-black-sea-initiative) | United Nations in Ukraine | 2023-05-17 | source type: UN press remarks | confidence: high | final evidence use: diplomacy, de-escalation, humanitarian relief | language: English | locator: page heading and date | supported claims: Russia confirmed another 60 days of participation; Russia, Ukraine, Türkiye, and UN kept discussing issues; the deal mattered for food security and global price stability | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect through Russian decision on participation | limitations: UN framing, not Russian position | contrary considerations: highlights continuing negotiation and constructive engagement | lenses: L1, L4, L7, L10
- `S042` [Humanitarians reached 7.3 million people in Ukraine with vital aid in the first six months of 2023](https://ukraine.un.org/en/240070-humanitarians-reached-73-million-people-ukraine-vital-aid-first-six-months-2023) | United Nations in Ukraine / OCHA | 2023-07-22 | source type: humanitarian situation note | confidence: high | final evidence use: civilian harm, humanitarian access, accountability, net-war-impact | language: English | locator: page heading and date | supported claims: Russia’s termination of the Black Sea Initiative and attacks on Odesa coincided with a worsening humanitarian situation; 7.3 million people received aid in H1 2023; access in Russian-controlled areas remained heavily impeded | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect through Russian military/state actions and access constraints | limitations: humanitarian actor perspective, not a legal judgment | contrary considerations: also documents substantial aid delivery and mitigation | lenses: L4, L5, L9, L10
- `S043` [Implementation of Ukrainian Peace Formula to make it possible to proceed to diplomatic fixation of end of war](https://www.president.gov.ua/en/news/vikonannya-ukrayinskoyi-formuli-miru-dast-zmogu-perejti-do-d-81245) | President of Ukraine | 2023-02-24 | source type: presidential statement | confidence: high | final evidence use: lawful settlement pathway, diplomacy, contrary evidence | language: English | locator: `turn17view0` L197-L214 | supported claims: Ukraine framed peace as requiring implementation of the Peace Formula, international law, security guarantees, and broad participation including China and India | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect, as the counterparty to the proposed settlement | limitations: Ukrainian government advocacy document | contrary considerations: rejects negotiated peace without territorial restoration and security guarantees | lenses: L1, L7, L10
- `S044` [The most important outcome of the meeting in Jeddah is that we are one step closer to the implementation of the Peace Formula - Andriy Yermak](https://www.president.gov.ua/en/news/najvazhlivishij-pidsumok-zustrichi-v-dzhiddi-mi-stali-she-na-84777) | President of Ukraine | 2023-08-08 | source type: presidential-office statement | confidence: high | final evidence use: diplomacy, mediation-party record, contrary evidence to “no talks” narratives | language: English | locator: `turn18view2` L203-L215 | supported claims: broad support for the Peace Formula grew; participants emphasized no freezing of the war; China continued in the format; consultations expanded | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect, because it addresses the war’s diplomatic end-state | limitations: Ukrainian diplomatic advocacy | contrary considerations: rejects frozen-conflict outcomes and frames Russian withdrawal as necessary | lenses: L1, L7, L10
- `S045` [Our Peace Formula gradually, step by step, is becoming global – address by the President of Ukraine](https://www.president.gov.ua/en/news/nasha-formula-miru-postupovo-krok-za-krokom-staye-globalnoyu-86669) | President of Ukraine | 2023-10-28 | source type: presidential address | confidence: high | final evidence use: diplomacy, lawful settlement, international coordination | language: English | locator: `turn18view4` L205-L214 | supported claims: 66 countries were represented; work was underway on five of ten formula points; the framework was presented as a global peace architecture against aggression | temporal fit: direct 2023 | Putin attribution: indirect as the conflict party the formula seeks to constrain | limitations: Ukrainian leadership advocacy | contrary considerations: explicitly frames Russia as aggressor and peace as contingent on territorial restoration | lenses: L1, L7, L10

**2B.1–2B.10 Lens Table**
| Lens | Accepted source IDs | Strongest favorable evidence | Strongest adverse evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1 diplomacy and de-escalation | S028, S036, S037, S038, S039, S040, S041, S043, S044, S045 | S028, S037-S045 show UN/Ukraine peace processes, grain corridor diplomacy, and lawful settlement framing | S001-S006 and S034 show continued coercion and wartime harm undercutting de-escalation |
| L2 initiation, expansion, prolongation, annexation, coercion, proxy conflict | S001-S006, S026, S027, S034, S036 | S036 and S027 provide Russia’s own defensive/administrative framing; S026 shows occupied-territory consolidation | S001-S006 and S034 show child transfer, torture, occupation governance, and continued escalation |
| L3 defensive necessity vs prestige/nationalism/diversion/regime survival | S026, S027, S036 | S036 frames Russia as defending sovereignty; S027 frames mobilization as state necessity | S026 and S034 point toward occupation consolidation and war-legitimation rather than pure defense |
| L4 civilian protection and humanitarian law | S001-S006, S028, S034, S037, S038, S039, S040, S041, S042 | S006, S028, S042 document aid, POW access, and humanitarian mitigation | S001-S005 and S034 document civilian harm, coercion, and IHL concerns |
| L5 restraint and responsibility for forces/proxies/allies/arms recipients | S001-S006, S026, S027, S028, S034, S036, S042 | S006, S028, S042 show restraint, humanitarian access, and mitigation channels | S001-S006, S034, S027 show coercive state control, mobilization, and operational responsibility failures |
| L6 truthful vs manipulative public justification | S026, S028, S036 | S026 and S036 preserve Putin/Russian public justifications in primary form; useful for comparison | S028 and S034 expose the gap between official rhetoric and observed coercion/harm |
| L7 ceasefires, negotiations, lawful settlements, reconciliation | S006, S028, S037, S038, S039, S040, S041, S043, S044, S045 | S028 and S037-S045 show active negotiations, grain-deal diplomacy, and lawful settlement proposals | S001-S006 and S034 show the war’s continuation despite diplomacy |
| L8 military spending and mobilization motives | S027 | S027 shows mobilization administration and state readiness rhetoric | S027 also evidences manpower extraction and war sustainment, so it cuts against a purely defensive reading |
| L9 accountability for failures, civilian harm, illegal conduct | S001-S006, S028, S034, S042 | S028 and S042 foreground accountability and humanitarian response; OSCE/OHCHR reports document violations | S001-S006 and S034 provide the strongest evidence of civilian harm and unlawful conduct |
| L10 net change in regional and international peace, stability, legality | All 20 accepted sources | S028, S037-S045, S042, S006 show mitigation, diplomacy, and humanitarian relief | S001-S006, S026, S034, S027, S036 show escalation, occupation, coercion, and war-sustaining policy |

**Counts**
- Raw candidates encountered: 115
- Verified unique canonical candidate URLs: 109
- Documents successfully opened: 31
- Final accepted source documents: 20
- Context-only sources: 17
- Access blocked: 12
- Opened-but-demoted: 11
- Rejected by reason at source-audit stage: 5 duplicate-family, 6 mirror/reprint, 0 irrelevant
- No accepted source is a mirror, duplicate-family item, snippet-only item, or filler

**Duplicate / Removal Audit**
- Duplicate-family removals:
  - `S029` duplicates the OSCE child-transfer family already represented by `S001`
  - `S030` duplicates the OSCE torture/sexual-violence family already represented by `S002`
  - `S031` duplicates the OHCHR April 2023 update already represented by `S004`
  - `S032` duplicates the OHCHR December 2023 civilians report already represented by `S005`
  - `S033` duplicates the ICRC operational report already represented by `S006`
- Mirror / reprint removals:
  - `S023`, `S024`, `S035`, `S046`, `S047`, `S048` were reprint/mirror-only recoveries and were removed because they added no unique underlying content beyond higher-authority or non-mirror documents
- No irrelevant cluster survived into the final accepted set

**Remaining Gaps / Saturation**
- Strong saturation on civilian harm, occupation coercion, diplomacy, humanitarian mitigation, and Russian public justification.
- Partial saturation on mobilization and war-sustainment motives.
- Remaining weak spots are direct 2023 Russian fiscal/budget primary text and more Kremlin transcript coverage. I targeted those, but the Kremlin/publication pages timed out and stayed access-blocked, so I did not accept them.
- Russian-language primary material is still thinner than ideal, but the chapter now has enough high-value evidence to cover all ten lenses without padding.
